title: Comparative Effects of Hormone Replacement Therapy and Exercise on Bone Health in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review
claims: Roughly 82 million women in the United States are in perimenopause, menopause or postmenopause.
Menopause typically occurs at a median age of 51 years in the United States, with approximately 1.3 million women transitioning into menopause annually.
Bone loss can begin before menopause and continues at a rate of 3% to 5% annually in the first five to seven years after menopause.
Vasomotor symptoms and a heightened long-term risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease often accompany the menopause transition.
Hormone replacement therapy provides the greatest bone-protective benefit when started before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, the so-called timing hypothesis.
Hormone replacement therapy is currently the most effective intervention for managing vasomotor symptoms.

Transdermal estradiol is associated with a lower risk of venous thromboembolism and stroke than oral estrogen, and micronized progesterone carries a lower breast cancer risk than synthetic progestins, although risks vary by formulation and route.
Weight-bearing exercise less than three times per week was associated with an increased risk of falls and hip fractures in one study cited by the review.

Impact loading exercise has shown statistically significant effects on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women across several meta-analyses, and resistance-based or mixed-loading programmes also improved bone mineral density.
This review included six studies and is a synthesis of selected evidence, not a clinical guideline.
